stories.title: Earthquake Destroys Japan Mall Just Weeks After It Reopened
stories.headline_kid: A huge earthquake shook southern Japan and part of a shopping mall collapsed, with rescue teams working hard to find everyone safe.
summary: On Tuesday, a powerful magnitude-7.1 earthquake struck Kumamoto, a region in southern Japan. Imagine a giant invisible hand shaking the ground so hard that roads crack and the power in thousands of homes goes out - that's how strong this quake was.

The earthquake hit an Aeon Mall shopping centre, and its second floor collapsed. There was also what sounded like an explosion, making the damage worse. Rescue workers have been digging through the rubble for two days. Sadly, two young women were found dead, a few more people are in critical condition, and around 10 people are still missing.

This particular mall had only just reopened last month, after being completely rebuilt following a deadly earthquake in the same area back in 2016. People had proudly called it a 'fresh start' - but it was destroyed again just weeks later.

Japan sits where several of the Earth's giant rock plates meet, which is why earthquakes happen there so often. Many Singaporean families travel to Japan for holidays, so people here are watching the news closely to make sure their loved ones are safe.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a Japan trip, this is a good reminder to learn safety steps like moving away from windows and heavy shelves during a quake.
lenses.family: Parents with relatives or holiday plans in Japan may be checking news updates and travel advisories closely right now.
lenses.friends: Classmates who love Japanese food, anime or theme parks might have questions about what really happens during an earthquake.
lenses.nation: Singapore rarely feels earthquakes since we're not near fault lines, but our buildings are still built to handle our own risks, like heavy rain and flooding.
lenses.world: It shows how disasters can strike suddenly, even in a place that had just finished rebuilding, reminding countries everywhere to keep improving safety standards.

stories.title: Singapore May Give Property Agents Star Ratings, Just Like Restaurants
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is planning new rules for property agents - including a rating system, just like the reviews you see for restaurants!
summary: When people buy or sell a home in Singapore, they often get help from a property agent - someone whose job is to guide buyers and sellers through the whole process, a bit like a matchmaker for houses.

Now, Singapore's Council for Estate Agencies (CEA) wants agents to complete a minimum number of property deals to keep working in the industry. This makes sure agents have real experience, similar to how a driving instructor needs enough practice before teaching others.

CEA is also studying whether to introduce consumer ratings for agents, like the star ratings you see for hawker stalls or delivery apps. This would let customers rate how helpful and honest their agent was, so future buyers can pick someone trustworthy.

Property agencies mostly welcome these plans but want safeguards, such as making sure ratings are fair and not misused. If these changes go ahead, buying or selling a home in Singapore could become safer and clearer for everyone.

lenses.me: If your family ever buys a new home, an agent with a good rating could make the whole process much smoother for everyone.
lenses.family: Parents looking to buy, sell or rent a flat or house will have more information to choose a reliable agent.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose parents work as agents might talk about how these new rules could affect their family's job.
lenses.nation: This shows Singapore working hard to keep its property market honest and trustworthy for all citizens.
lenses.world: Other countries dealing with property scams or unqualified agents might look at Singapore's rating idea as a model to copy.

stories.title: 335 Scammers Arrested Just Next Door to Singapore
stories.headline_kid: Police in Johor arrested 335 people running online scams from a giant complex only a short drive from Singapore!
summary: Police in Johor Bahru, Malaysia, have busted two big scam gangs operating out of Forest City, a large development in Iskandar Puteri that's only about a 30-minute drive from Singapore.

The suspects, aged between 20 and 58, came from several countries including China, Indonesia and Myanmar. They are believed to have worked in organised groups, using phone calls and messages to trick victims from other countries out of their money.

This kind of crime is called a 'scam syndicate' - a group of people working together to cheat others, often hiding behind fake identities or fake investment offers. Because Forest City is so close to Singapore, some of these scam calls could have targeted people here too.

The arrest of 335 suspects shows how seriously Malaysia is cracking down on scam operations near the border. It's a good reminder for everyone, including kids, to be careful of strange calls or messages asking for money or personal information.

lenses.me: This reminds you to never give away personal information or passwords, even if a message sounds urgent or official-sounding.
lenses.family: Parents should stay alert to scam calls, especially ones pretending to be from banks or government offices.
lenses.friends: Classmates can share this story to remind each other that 'stranger danger' also applies to phone calls and texts, not just people in person.
lenses.nation: Singapore works closely with Malaysia to fight cross-border scams, since scammers often hide just across the Causeway.
lenses.world: It shows how scam syndicates operate across many countries, meaning nations need to cooperate to catch them.

stories.title: Malaysia's Weather Experts Warn of a Drier Season Next Door
stories.headline_kid: Johor and Melaka could get up to 40% less rain later this year - and that might matter for Singapore too!
summary: Malaysia's weather agency, MetMalaysia, says that Johor and Melaka - the states right next to Singapore - might get 20 to 40 per cent less rain than usual during the Northeast Monsoon, a rainy season that usually runs from around November to March.

This is because of El Nino, a natural weather pattern where parts of the Pacific Ocean become warmer than usual. Think of El Nino like a giant weather 'switch' that changes rainfall across many parts of Asia, sometimes bringing dry spells to places that are usually wet.

Less rain in Johor matters to Singapore because we get some of our water supply from Johor's rivers. Drier weather could also mean hazier or warmer days spreading into Singapore, since our two countries share the same regional climate.
Experts are watching closely so that both countries can prepare early, such as saving water and planning ahead, well before the dry season actually arrives.

lenses.me: You might notice hotter, drier days later this year, so remember to drink more water and wear a hat when you're outdoors.
lenses.family: Families might see reminders to save water at home if supplies become tighter in the coming months.
lenses.friends: Classmates learning about climate in school will find this a real-life example of what they study in Geography lessons.
lenses.nation: Singapore relies partly on water from Johor, so this news affects how much we may need to depend on our own reservoirs and NEWater.
lenses.world: This shows how El Nino, a global weather event, connects countries thousands of kilometres apart through shared weather systems.

stories.title: Singapore's Bars Shine on Asia's Top 50 List Again
stories.headline_kid: Singapore landed four spots on Asia's list of top 50 bars - proof our food and drink scene is world-class!
summary: Every year, food and drink experts across Asia vote for the best bars in the region, a bit like how movies get nominated for awards. This year, for the first time, a bar from Guangzhou, China called Hope & Sesame took the number one spot.

Singapore did well too, with four of our bars making it onto the top 50 list, showing our food and drink scene is respected across Asia. However, Singapore's previous top bar, Jigger & Pony, slipped down to No. 9 this year.

Other cities like Seoul, Hong Kong, Bangkok and several Chinese cities also had strong showings, with 14 completely new bars appearing on the list. The competition celebrates creative bartenders, called mixologists, who compete to invent the tastiest and most original drinks.

While the drinks themselves are for adults, this achievement matters because it puts Singapore on the map as a place known for creativity, hospitality and excellent service - the same qualities that make our hawker food and restaurants famous worldwide too.

lenses.me: Even if you can't try these drinks yet, you can feel proud that Singapore is known worldwide for creativity in food and drink.
lenses.family: Parents who enjoy going out for special occasions might recognise some of these award-winning spots.
lenses.friends: Classmates who love cooking shows might find it interesting that bartenders compete like chefs do, inventing new creations.
lenses.nation: This shows Singapore continues to shine in global rankings for hospitality, boosting our reputation as a food and lifestyle destination.
lenses.world: It highlights how Asian cities, especially in China, are becoming major players in global dining and drinks culture, not just Western cities like London or New York.
